title: English Grammar and Clear Writing Essentials
summary: Learn the grammar, punctuation and editing habits that make your writing correct, clear and ready for school, university and work.
audience: Secondary and university students who want stronger grammar and clearer writing in formal English

body.p: Every word in a sentence does a job. The job is called its part of speech, and knowing the main ones helps you build and repair sentences. The same word can do different jobs: in 'Please water the plants', water is a verb, but in 'The water is clean' it is a noun. Always look at how the word is used.

list: Noun: names a person, place, thing or idea (Amina, Freetown, book, honesty).
Pronoun: replaces a noun (she, them, it, ours, who).
Verb: shows an action or state (run, write, is, seem).
Adjective: describes a noun (a heavy bag, three students).
Adverb: describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb, often answering how, when or where (quickly, very, yesterday).
Preposition: links a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence, often showing place or time (in, on, at, under, after).
Conjunction: joins words or clauses (and, but, because, although).
Determiner: introduces a noun (a, the, this, my, some).

body.p: Worked example: 'Kwame quickly finished his very difficult homework before dinner.' Kwame is a noun and the subject. Quickly is an adverb describing finished. Finished is a verb. His is a determiner. Very is an adverb describing difficult. Difficult is an adjective describing homework. Homework is a noun. Before is a preposition, and dinner is a noun.

When you know that an adjective describes a noun and an adverb describes a verb, you can fix common mistakes. 'She sings beautiful' is wrong because sings is a verb, so it needs an adverb: 'She sings beautifully'. In contrast, 'She looks beautiful' is correct because looks here is a linking verb that connects the subject to a description, and so it takes an adjective.

body.tip: To test a word, ask what question it answers. If it tells you which one or what kind, it is an adjective. If it tells you how, when or where, it is probably an adverb.

body.p: Spelling note: British English writes colour, favourite, organise and centre. American English writes color, favorite, organize and center. Both are correct in their own country. Choose one style for each piece of writing and keep to it. This course uses the British forms.

A sentence needs a subject (who or what the sentence is about) and a verb (what the subject does or is), and it must express a complete thought. A group of words with its own subject and verb is a clause. A clause that can stand alone is an independent clause. A clause that cannot stand alone, usually starting with words like because, although, when or who, is a dependent clause.

list: Simple: one independent clause. 'The bus arrived.'
Compound: two independent clauses joined by a conjunction such as and, but or so. 'The bus arrived, and we climbed aboard.'
Complex: one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. 'We climbed aboard because the rain had started.'
Compound-complex: two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. 'The bus arrived, and we climbed aboard because the rain had started.'

body.p: A fragment is a piece that is not a full sentence: 'Because the rain had started.' It has a subject and a verb but the word because makes it dependent. A run-on or comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma: 'The bus arrived, we climbed aboard.' Fix it with a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction.

A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. In the present tense, the singular form usually ends in -s: 'The student writes', 'The students write'. Find the real subject and ignore the words between it and the verb.

list: 'The list of names is on the board.' The subject is list, not names.
'Each of the girls has a ticket.' Each is singular.
'Amina and Kofi are in the choir.' Two subjects joined by and are plural.
'The team plays well.' In British English a team may also be treated as plural ('The team are tired'); in a formal exam, treating it as singular is the safer choice.
'There are three reasons.' The subject comes after the verb, so check it.

body.tip: When a sentence feels confusing, cross out the extra phrase. 'The results of the examination (is/are) ready' becomes 'The results are ready'. Now the plural subject results is clear.

body.p: Tense tells the reader when something happens. Choosing the right tense and keeping it consistent makes your meaning clear. The three time zones are past, present and future, and each has simple, continuous and perfect forms.

body.code:
Simple present     I walk to school.
Present continuous I am walking to school now.
Present perfect    I have walked to school every day this term.
Simple past        I walked to school yesterday.
Past continuous    I was walking when it began to rain.
Past perfect       I had walked ten minutes before the bus passed.
Simple future      I will walk tomorrow.
Future continuous  I will be walking at six o'clock.

list: Simple present is for habits and general facts: 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.'
Present continuous is for actions happening now or around now: 'She is revising for her exams.'

Present perfect links the past to now, and is used when the exact time is not given: 'I have finished my essay.' Do not use it with a finished time word: 'I have finished yesterday' is wrong; write 'I finished yesterday'.
Past perfect shows which of two past events came first: 'When we arrived, the match had started.' The match started first.
Future can be shown with will, or with going to: 'I will call you' or 'I am going to call you'.

body.p: Worked example of consistency. Wrong: 'Last Friday we visit the market and bought some mangoes.' The first verb is present while the second is past. Right: 'Last Friday we visited the market and bought some mangoes.' Keep one time frame unless the meaning really changes.

Irregular verbs do not take -ed in the past. Go becomes went and has gone, write becomes wrote and has written, and teach becomes taught. Note that the past participle (the form used after have) is sometimes different from the simple past: 'I saw it' but 'I have seen it'.

body.tip: For facts that are always true, use the present even inside a past story: 'The teacher explained that the Earth orbits the Sun.'

body.p: The articles are a, an and the. A and an are indefinite: they point to any one example of something. The is definite: it points to a particular one that the speaker and reader both know. Compare 'I need a pen' (any pen) with 'I need the pen on your desk' (a specific one).

The choice depends on the sound that follows, not the spelling. Use an before a vowel sound and a before a consonant sound. So we say an apple, an hour (the h is silent) and an MP (the letter M is said 'em'). We say a university (it begins with a 'yoo' sound), a European tour and a one-day trip (it begins with 'wun').

list: Use the for something already mentioned: 'I bought a book. The book was cheap.'
Use the for something unique: the sun, the Internet, the Prime Minister.
Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns: 'Students need sleep.' 'Water is essential.'

Use the with the names of rivers, oceans and some countries with plural or 'Republic' names: the Volta, the Atlantic, the Gambia, the United Kingdom. Most countries and cities take no article: Kenya, Zambia, Spain, Dublin.

body.p: Prepositions show relationships of place, time and direction. Many go with particular words and have to be learned together. Common correct combinations are: interested in, good at, depend on, afraid of, listen to, different from, arrive at a building, arrive in a city or country, and married to.

body.code:
Time:   at 6 o'clock, on Monday, in June, in 2026
Place:  at the bus stop, on the table, in the classroom
Wrong:  She is married with a doctor.   Right: She is married to a doctor.
Wrong:  It depends of the weather.      Right: It depends on the weather.
Wrong:  I am good in maths.             Right: I am good at maths.

body.p: The pattern for time is: use at for exact clock times, on for days and dates, and in for longer periods such as months, years and seasons. Learn each verb or adjective with its preposition, as a unit, instead of translating from another language.

lessons.title: Punctuation: commas, apostrophes, semicolons and colons

body.p: Punctuation shows the reader where the pauses and links are. Small marks can change meaning. 'Let's eat, Grandma' invites her to dinner, while 'Let's eat Grandma' does not. We will look at four marks that cause the most trouble.

list: Separate items in a list: 'We bought rice, beans, plantain and oil.'
Put a comma after an introductory phrase: 'After the lesson, we went home.'
Use a comma before a conjunction joining two independent clauses: 'The exam was hard, but I finished.'
Put commas around extra information that could be removed: 'My cousin, who lives in Lusaka, is a nurse.'
Do not use a comma alone to join two independent clauses. That is a comma splice.

body.p: An apostrophe shows possession or a missing letter. For one owner, add 's: the student's book. For a plural ending in s, add the apostrophe after the s: the students' books means books belonging to several students. For plurals not ending in s, add 's: the children's room. Contractions use an apostrophe where letters are missing: do not becomes don't and it is becomes it's. Never use an apostrophe to make a plural: write 'two bananas', not 'two banana's'. Possessive pronouns (yours, hers, its, ours, theirs) never take an apostrophe.

A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses: 'Lamin loves football; his sister prefers netball.' Both halves could stand alone. It can also separate items in a list when the items already contain commas. A colon introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation after a complete clause: 'You need three things: a pen, a ruler and a calculator.' What comes before a colon must be able to stand alone as a sentence.

body.tip: Wrong: 'I need: a pen and a ruler.' Right: 'I need a pen and a ruler.' or 'I need two things: a pen and a ruler.'

body.p: American English puts commas and full stops inside closing quotation marks, while British usage often places them according to the meaning. Both are accepted in their regions.
Some mistakes appear in the work of even strong writers because the words sound alike or look alike. Learn the pairs below and you remove a large share of errors from your writing.

list: its / it's: its is possessive ('The school lost its roof'). It's is short for it is or it has ('It's raining').
their / there / they're: their shows ownership ('their books'), there shows place or is used in 'there is' ('Put it there'), and they're means they are ('They're late').
your / you're: your shows ownership; you're means you are.
affect / effect: affect is usually a verb meaning to influence ('Noise affects my sleep'). Effect is usually a noun meaning a result ('Noise has an effect on my sleep').
fewer / less: fewer is for things you can count ('fewer students'). Less is for quantities that are not counted one by one ('less water', 'less time').
then / than: then is about time ('First wash, then dry'). Than is for comparison ('taller than her').
to / too / two: to is a preposition or part of a verb ('to school'), too means also or excessively ('too hot'), two is the number.
practice / practise: in British English practice is the noun and practise is the verb ('I practise every day; the practice is useful'). American English uses practice for both.

body.p: Worked example. Wrong: 'Their going to loose there chance if the effect them.' Right: 'They're going to lose their chance if it affects them.' Notice three different corrections: they're, lose (loose means not tight), and affects.

Say the full form aloud. If 'it is' or 'it has' fits where you wrote it's, the apostrophe is right. If it does not fit, you need its. In the same way, try 'they are' for they're. For affect and effect, ask whether you need an action word, which is affect, or a thing, which is effect. If you can put 'the' or 'an' before the word, the noun effect is the safe choice.

body.tip: Keep your own list of mistakes. Whenever a teacher marks one, add it to the list and check each new piece of writing against it. Spelling checkers often miss these errors because every word is a real word.

lessons.title: Sentence variety, clear paragraphs and editing

body.p: Good writing is not only correct, it is also easy and pleasant to read. Three habits help: vary your sentences, build clear paragraphs, and edit your own work in a careful second pass.

A text made only of short sentences sounds choppy: 'The market was busy. Traders shouted. Buyers argued. The sun was hot.' A text made only of long sentences tires the reader. Mix them. Join related ideas with conjunctions, start some sentences with a phrase, and use a short sentence for emphasis. Revised: 'The market was busy, with traders shouting and buyers arguing under the hot sun. Nobody noticed the time.'

A paragraph deals with one main idea. It usually begins with a topic sentence that states the idea. The following sentences give explanation, evidence or an example, and the last sentence closes or links to the next paragraph. Start a new paragraph when you move to a new idea.

body.code:
Topic sentence: Regular practice improves handwriting.
Support:        Students who copy a page each day form letters more evenly.
Example:        After a month, Fatmata's writing was easier to read.
Closing:        Small daily effort therefore brings visible progress.

body.p: Use linking words to guide the reader: first, however, for example, as a result, in addition, finally. Use them where they carry real meaning, not on every line.

steps: Leave a gap. Wait at least a short time, ideally until the next day, before you edit, because you will see what you wrote and not what you meant.
Read it aloud, slowly. Your ear catches missing words and awkward sentences that your eye skips.
Check one problem at a time: first the meaning and order, then the sentences, then agreement and tense, and finally spelling and punctuation.
Cut the unnecessary. 'Due to the fact that' can become 'because'.
Check against your personal list of common errors, then read it once more from the last sentence to the first to catch typing slips.

body.tip: If you write on a phone, turn on the spelling checker but do not trust it completely. It will accept 'their' where you needed 'there', because both are real words.

quiz.q: In the sentence 'The students listened carefully', which word is an adverb?
options: carefully
students
listened
The

quiz.q: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The box of pencils are on the shelf.
The boxes of pencil is on the shelf.
The box of pencils is on the shelf.
The box of pencils were on the shelf.

quiz.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: We stayed indoors, and the rain was heavy.
We stayed indoors because the rain was heavy.
The rain was heavy.
We stayed indoors, but the rain stopped.
When we arrived at the hall, the lesson already starts.
When we arrive at the hall, the lesson had already started.
When we had arrived at the hall, the lesson already started.
When we arrived at the hall, the lesson had already started.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses an article correctly?
options: She is studying at an university in Ghana.
She is studying at a university in the Ghana.
She is studying at the an university in Ghana.
She is studying at a university in Ghana.

quiz.q: Which preposition completes the sentence correctly? 'My results depend ___ my revision.'
options: of
on
at
from

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly to talk about the books of several students?
options: The students' books were on the desk.
The student's books were on the desk.
The students book's were on the desk.
The studentses books were on the desk.

quiz.q: Which choice is correct? 'The dog wagged ___ tail.'
options: it's
its'
its
it is
Amina loves reading, her brother prefers football.
Amina loves reading; and her brother prefers football.
Amina loves reading; her brother prefers football.
Amina loves: reading her brother prefers football.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
options: Bring three things: a pen, a ruler and a calculator.
Bring: a pen, a ruler and a calculator.
Please bring a: pen, ruler and calculator.
Bring three things; a pen, a ruler and a calculator.
Too much noise can effect your concentration.
Too much noise can have an affect on your concentration.
Two much noise can affect you're concentration.
Too much noise can affect your concentration.
There are less chairs than students, so we have fewer space.
There are fewer chairs than students, so we have less space.
There are fewer chairs then students, so we have less space.
There is fewer chairs than students, so we have less space.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? '___ going to bring ___ books to the library over ___.'
options: Their, they're, there
They're, their, there
There, their, they're
They're, there, their

quiz.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
options: The exam finished early, so we went home.
After the exam finished early, we went home.
The exam finished early; we went home.
The exam finished early, we went home.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a topic sentence in a paragraph?
options: To repeat the title of the whole essay
To give the final conclusion of the essay
To state the main idea that the rest of the paragraph develops
To list every example in the paragraph

quiz.q: You have finished a draft of an essay and the deadline is tomorrow. Which editing approach is most effective?
options: Leave it for a while, then read it aloud and check one type of problem at a time
Submit it at once because the first draft expresses your ideas best
Run a spelling checker only, since it finds all errors
Change every long sentence into a short one
